Q: How can I work parallel in unity with my friend? A:

We use git for Unity and Unreal Engine projects and we have quite the experience with that. I recommend it, but with a caveat: you need a developer who knows or is willing to learn git.

So, a couple of things to be aware of:

  • git was not designed for these kind projects (games). So there are a couple of oddities and awkward kinks and lacking in the quality of life department.
  • you MUST use git LFS
  • correctly configuring LFS with Unity can be a bit tricky. For instance most of .asset are in text format, but there are exceptions, like LightingData.asset which are binary. There are a myriad of file types Unity uses, there isn't a complete list of them and you don't know if they are binary or text. As your project grows you will encounter more and more filetypes and you have to manually check if they are text or binary. This is made worse by the fact that git doesn't offer a user friendly way of showing new file types added to the repo, or how it tracks current files. We use a custom script for this. We also have a long list of file types put together over the years and we constantly find new file types we haven't encountered before. Oh and did I mentioned that some filetypes sometimes are text and sometimes are binary?
  • Git Hosting services (like github or gitlab) are pretty expensive for LFS (and don't allow repos larger than 100MB, so you have to use LFS). When we searched our provider a couple of years ago we found https://bitbucket.org/ to be by far the cheapest. I don't know how the situation changed since then. Unity projects can be pretty small though and you might find free storage for your needs.
  • git is excellent for collaboration on code files. So you both can work on the same C# scripts at the same time with no problem if you know a bit of git.
  • while Unity scene files are text and theoretically git can merge unity scenes, I strongly advise against this. Don't work in parallel on the same scene! However this is not as big of a problem as it sounds. Use prefabs and this way you both practically work on the same scene, as long as each of you works on a different prefab.
  • do NOT work on the same binary files at the same time. There is no way to merge the files keeping work from both people. You will have to pick one edit and discard the work of the other person. Again, with minimal discipline and communication this is not a problem at all.
  • do NOT use git flow, especially since you are new to git. It's a complex workflow of branches and merging strategies designed for programming projects.
  • use a single main branch and pull (merge) and push often. To a non game developer this might look like bad advice. But we found this is the best strategy for game development, especially for you since you are not familiar with git.
  • do NOT rebase (unless you know what you are doing).
  • commit often
  • pull (merge) and push often. At least once a day. You need to minimize the chance of a conflict in your files. You do not want to work locally for a week and then find out you have a conflict. While this would not be a problem with git on programming project (so it's ok to do this on C# files) it definitely can be a huge headache for game asset files.
  • pull (merge) and push often! At least once a day.
  • pull (merge) and push often!! At least once a day.
  • keep in mind git is 100% not friendly to artists. You need in the team at least one developer who knows git.
  • you don't need to use the command line. There are fully featured standalone git GUI out there. We use SourceTree from Atlassiann because from what we've tried we found it's the most friendly to people who don't know git.
  • definitely take your time to learn the git basics. There might be daunting at first, but it's worth on the long term.
  • don't be afraid to ask your friendly neighbor LLM chat how to do that git thing you don't know how to do. But definitely learn the basics first!

Unity has a proprietary alternative: Unity Version Control (previously called Plastic SCM). We've tried it on a couple of projects, but we returned to git every single time. I want to stress out that the reason WE returned to git is because we have on our team someone who knows git pretty well (me 😁), nobody that knows Unity Version Control well and I am always there to get us out of the pickles git puts us in. We also use git for Unreal Engine projects anyway. For other teams and maybe for you Unity version control might be worth considering.

There are other alternatives designed specifically with games in mind like Perforce Helix Core or Diversion source control but we never tried them.

Whatever you choose, choose a source control system. Do NOT use anything else, like for instance file sharing services (google drive, onedrive etc.), or even shared local networks. They are fine to share some assets, but absolutely terrible to collaborate on a game project. (yes, we've had a client who insisted on using google drive instead of git... for a ~60 GB Unreal Engine project... with a 4 persons team... yeah...)

Git is awesome

I know all of this might seem daunting and might scare you from using git. So I want to rightfully push the needle in the other direction. Here are the good awesome things about git:

Git (and all alternatives) are not just a collaborative tool. They bring so much more value to your work. I use git for every project or stub of project I start, even if I am soloing it and never plan to host it anywhere.

The best undo ever

With git I never worry about losing my work, the program crashing, bugs corrupting files or messing up something myself. Commit often and you always have a very recent snapshot of the project and hundreds, even thousand of snapshots of your project going all the way back to the state where you just created a new empty project.

Need to upgrade (Unity, a plugin, or a package)? Afraid of the upgrade breaking the project? Not with git. If anything bad happens, I can do the upgrade all over again until I get it right, or if nothing fixes it, stay on the previous version.

UE's auto save feature takes a long time and it freezes the editor while doing that. The only problem I have with that is that I have to disable it for each new UE update.

Experiment without fear

Trying something you don't know where is going or if you will end up keeping it? Afraid of messing up what you already have? Not with git! You can work on experiments on a different branch, or you can simply not commit and discard everything, or go back to a commit before the experiment.

Play the blame game (in the best possible way)

Want to see who wrote that line of code? Or when? IDEs have baked in git blame support. See at a glance the last one that modified each line of code and the name of the commit.

Find the source of bugs

You've worked for quite some time on one portion of the game and now you try something you haven't tried in a long time and ... horror: something that worked previously now is broken. You don't know what you did that broke it. You don't remember when was the last time it worked fine.

With git: no problem. Git bisect and find fast the exact commit that broke that feature. Now you know exactly what modifications introduced the bug.

Bring old assets back or even entire scenes

You've had a version of some assets, edited them and now you want to go back to the way it was. (Almost) no problem. Just get those specific assets from the old commit. It gets complicated if there are complex dependencies, but most of the time it works just fine.

Run and compare two versions of your game at the same time

Want to compare how your game runs now with a previous version? Side by side? Want to compare code from a previous version to the current one. Or two old version? Not a problem. With git worktree you can easily have two or more versions of your project on the disk at the same time.

Q: How do you usually organize Models, Controllers, and Routes in Laravel projects? A:

Depending on the size of the app you're trying to build, there is a few approaches. Laravel already has a fairly clear structure so I would suggest sticking to it at the start:

  • Models goes under app/Models,
  • Services under app/Services,
  • Routes goes under routes/{group}.php,
  • Controllers under app/Http/Controllers,
  • Migrations in database/migrations,
  • Etc.

It also help to use the tools that Laravel offers to reduce the amount of code needed in your "base" component. For example, use Resources rather than building a json object in your controller. Use FormRequest to validate your input data. Use Gates and Policies to handle permission and access check. Use services and repository rather than handling business logic and database access in your Controllers.

All of this will help you lighten your Models and Controllers, and are all tools offered by Laravel from the get go.

Then, as your project evolve, you could consider splitting it into "smaller laravel project". In our case, we created a folder named "Domains", right under app, which contains 1 sub folder for each domain of the app.

.
└── app/
    └── Domains/
        ├── FirstAppModule
        ├── SecondAppModule
        └── etc.

Each Domains has it's own directory structure which mimic the base Laravel structure.

.
└── app/
    └── Domains/
        └── FirstAppModule/
            ├── Http/
            │   ├── Controllers
            │   ├── Resources
            │   └── Requests
            ├── Models
            ├── Services
            ├── Policies
            ├── Migrations
            ├── Views
            └── ...

This has helped us a lot as our application grew because it made testing and developing much much easier.

And since laravel offer an extensive Package SDK, we could build each Domains as an individual "Laravel application" that could be isolated and deployed individually. This might not be needed in your case, but it's nice to know that it's possible.

In the end, there is no single perfect solution. It comes down to how you want to structure your project. The best tips I can give you is to stick to the Laravel Structure. It's well made and well known, which might help new developers understanding where things are.

Best of luck !

Q: Package installation ERROR: KeyError: key v"version" not found A:

A community member (Oliver Ahrend) brought up a simple solution on Julia's slack helpdesk. The solution was simply to update Julia.

Since I couldn't add packages, they recommended using the package, JuliaUP which is simple to use.

After updating Julia, I was able to install my packages.

It's worth noting that whatever caused this original issue is still unsolved; I assume some sort of breakage had happened in the registry.

Q: crbug/1173575, non-JS module files deprecated on Chrome Extension A:

to get rid of this error (crbug/1173575, non-JS module files deprecated.) I have to change the Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy in .htaccess file , found in Apache server's web folder, from "require-corp" to "cross-origin":


- Header set Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy "require-corp"
+ Header set Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy "cross-origin"

Q: Kill and restart ngrok within a shell script A:

If I am at all able to guess what you are trying to ask, run the new command in a subprocess. You are already doing that, albeit clumsily.

#!/bin/sh

ngrok_pid=$(pgrep ngrok)
echo "$0: Current ngrok PID = ${ngrok_pid}" >&2

if [ "$ngrok_pid" ] && kill -9 $ngrok_pid
then
    ( ./ngrok http 5000 & )
    # do more checks below...
else
    echo "$0: NO ngrok PID found" >&2
fi

This avoids testing “$?” to see if a command succeeded or not and the superfluous command substitution. if [ "$ngrok_pid" ] && avoids trying to run kill if there is no PID. Finally we take care to include the name of the script in its diagnotic messages, and printing them to standard error >&2 instead of standard output.

A better solution altogether might be to run ngrok as a service, and merely using cron to tell the service to restart; but how exactly to do that is system-dependent. Fortunately, the documentation has instructions for multiple popular architectures. Then, all you need in your cron job is

ngrok service restart

The original service should be launched at reboot or etc with something like

ngrok service install --config /etc/ngrok.yml

but I defer to the ngrok manual for details.
